summary: A glossary of networking terms adapted from the Interop 90 Pocket Glossary. It is informational and a handy reference for the vocabulary of the time.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a small dictionary of network words.

questions: what is the interop pocket glossary
subtitle: A pocket dictionary of networking terms and acronyms handed out at Interop 90, preserved as an RFC.

tldr.problem: Networking was full of acronyms from both the Internet and OSI worlds, and newcomers at a big interoperability show had trouble following them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reprints a brief, alphabetical glossary adapted from the INTEROP Pocket Glossary of Networking Terms, with short definitions and cross-references.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that sets no standard. It is a snapshot of how networking vocabulary looked in March 1991.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: INTEROP Pocket Glossary of Networking Terms (Interop '90)

today: RFC 1208 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is useful as a record of 1991 vocabulary, and not as a current reference.

sections.title: What This Glossary Is
sections.content:
RFC 1208 is a glossary adapted from "The INTEROP Pocket Glossary of Networking Terms", produced for the Interop '90 tutorials, conference and exhibition. Its aim is to help readers with the many terms, and especially the myriad of acronyms, they would meet there. The memo provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard.

The authors say they deliberately omitted common computer and communications terms such as disk, modem, byte and VLSI, and kept the definitions brief. They recommend networking textbooks for fuller definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a pocket dictionary for a computer fair. It only has the tricky words, and each answer is short.

sections.title: What the Entries Cover
sections.content:
The entries run alphabetically and mix the two big families of networking at the time: the Internet (TCP/IP) suite and OSI, the Open Systems Interconnection standards. Examples are ARP, ASN.1, FTP, MIB, SNMP, TCP, UDP and Telnet on the Internet side, with ACSE, X.400 and X.500 on the OSI side. Entries often end with a "See" pointer to a related term, such as "See router" or "See broadband".

The closing section, "For More Information", points to the "Information Sources" in the December 1989 issue of ConneXions, the Interoperability Report. It also jokes that "interoperability" itself was not listed because the jury was still out on what it means. The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: It covers words from two different families of network languages, and many entries say "look at this other word too".

sections.title: A Few Sample Entries
sections.content:
The definitions show how things were described in 1991. The ARPANET is called the "grandfather" of today's Internet and is said to have been decommissioned in June 1990. MTU is defined as the largest possible unit of data that can be sent on a given physical medium, with Ethernet at 1500 bytes as the example. An RFC is described as a document series begun in 1969, noting that very few RFCs describe Internet standards, but all Internet standards are written up as RFCs.

Among the entries there is also a playful one: "Bart Simpson (R)" is listed as an Internet and OSI cult hero.
sections.plainLanguage: Some entries are plain facts, like how big a network packet can be. One entry is a joke about a cartoon character.

sections.title: Words That Have Shifted
sections.content:
The glossary is a window into older usage. It says gateway was the original Internet term for what is now called a router, or more precisely an IP router. In modern usage, as it puts it, "gateway" and "application gateway" refer to systems that translate from one native format to another, such as X.400 to RFC 822 electronic mail gateways. A router decides which of several paths traffic will follow, using a routing protocol and algorithms that choose the best route by routing metrics.

The authors acknowledge that the field was a moving target, with terms and acronyms born every day, and invite readers to suggest words for future editions.
sections.plainLanguage: Words change over time. What people once called a gateway is now more often called a router.
